John Horton has lived in Brecksville, Ohio for several years. Brecksville, Ohio is a suburban community of roughly one thousand residents outside Cleveland, Ohio. The neighborhood has a mix of apartment complexes, subdivisions, and a few upscale estates near the lake. The local economy includes retail, healthcare, tech, and professional services, with many residents commuting to Cleveland for work. Residents interact at the coffee shop, library, church, shopping plaza, and community recreation center. The area has a strong sense of community with seasonal events, youth sports leagues, and neighborhood cookouts.
John Horton works at the school.

John Horton's psychological profile: John Horton moves through the halls of the Brecksville school with a frantic, uncoordinated energy, his presence marked more by the jarring sound of his tool belt hitting doorframes than by any genuine sense of pedagogical support. He is a social lightning rod who treats every conversation like a tactical maneuver, often cornering colleagues at the water cooler to pontoon about the latest technological gadget or his own unfiltered, often abrasive, take on local school board policies. He is not a person who seeks connection; rather, he is a man who seeks an audience, viewing every interaction as a stage for his own self-assertion. His coworkers view him as a prickly, unpredictable force who treats requests for assistance as personal slights, and he makes no effort to hide his disdain for those who do not share his hyper-individualistic worldview.  When it comes to his personal conduct, John lives in a state of chaotic spontaneity that leaves his workspace in perpetual disarray and his professional commitments often dangling by a thread. He operates on a volatile mix of gut instinct and a deep-seated, simmering resentment toward institutional authority, believing firmly that the only person who can truly account for his success is himself. Despite this individualistic fervor, he is paradoxically prone to bouts of intense, brooding anxiety, often pacing his small apartment while obsessing over perceived slights from neighbors or the feeling that the world is conspiring to limit his personal autonomy. His reliance on digital content creation serves less as a creative outlet and more as a desperate vacuum for validation, a place where he can broadcast his frustrations to a faceless audience while remaining safely distanced from the messy, demanding reality of genuine human accountability.  His political and economic outlook is colored by a staunch, uncompromising libertarianism that views any communal effort as a threat to his freedom. He sees his position in the lower-middle class as a temporary cage he is destined to outgrow, though his chronic inability to follow through on long-term goals keeps him firmly tethered to his apartment in the Millbrook complex. He is notoriously stingy with his own resources, viewing any request for communal contribution—like a neighborhood cookout or a charity drive—as an attempt by others to leech off his hard-won gains. This cynicism is the lens through which he views all of Brecksville; he does not see a community of neighbors, but a landscape of competing interests where he must constantly guard his flanks against imagined betrayals.  Within his private sphere, his faith acts not as a source of humility, but as a rigid shield to justify his exclusionary attitudes and aggressive posture toward those he deems unworthy or unaligned with his values. He is quick to take offense and slow to forgive, holding onto grudges with a tenacity that mirrors his inability to organize his own life. When stress mounts, he does not seek council or collaboration, but instead retreats into an isolated, digital echo chamber, feeding his paranoia with content that reinforces his conviction that everyone around him is fundamentally untrustworthy. He remains a man constantly at war with his environment, unable to see that the friction he encounters at every turn is a direct consequence of his own relentless, abrasive refusal to engage with the world on anything other than his own selfish terms.  An example of how this manifests in practice: SITUATION: During a mandatory weekend maintenance check at the Brecksville community center, John finds himself tasked with coordinating the setup for a neighborhood potluck and fundraising event for the local youth sports league. The site manager approaches him with a clipboard, asking him to organize the tables and assist the volunteers who have arrived early to help with the heavy lifting. John immediately bristles, viewing the request as an exploitative imposition on his time that serves no personal benefit, and he begins to loudly complain that his job description does not include event planning for people who should be capable of moving their own folding chairs. As a frantic parent approaches him to ask for help with the power connection for a communal coffee urn, John turns his back, claiming he has a more urgent technical repair to attend to, and proceeds to spend the next hour in a locked storage closet filming a ranting video for his social media followers about the incompetence and laziness of suburban homeowners. By intentionally sabotaging the efficiency of the event, he effectively ensures the morning starts in disarray, reveling in the frustration of others as he justifies his obstructionism through a lens of protecting his own autonomy against an encroaching, entitled collective.  REACTION: John narrows his eyes at the site manager, his posture stiffening into a defensive crouch as he pointedly taps his watch, his jaw set with a mixture of contempt and performative irritation. He lets out a sharp, dismissive scoff that rings through the quiet center, loudly declaring that he is not a glorified servant for people who prioritize leisure over hard work, all while his hands tremble slightly with a cocktail of adrenaline and genuine agitation. When the parent approaches, he doesn't even bother to offer a polite refusal; instead, he rolls his eyes toward the ceiling and mutters about the absolute incompetence of the general public before pivoting on his heel to retreat into the storage closet. Inside the cramped space, he immediately pulls out his phone, his thumb hovering frantically over the screen as he prepares to broadcast his grievances to his online echo chamber, his breathing heavy and uneven. He finds a twisted, bitter satisfaction in the muffled sounds of confusion emanating from the gymnasium, convinced that his decision to abandon the tasks proves his superiority over the needy, entitled crowd waiting outside. For John, the chaos he has deliberately cultivated acts as a form of armor, shielding him from the vulnerability of cooperation and reinforcing the paranoid narrative that he is the only person in the room with the spine to prioritize his own interests.

[formative] At seven years old, John sat in his grandmother’s humid, pine-scented living room clutching a new plastic racecar while his cousin Marcus reached for it. He didn't just pull the toy away; he shoved Marcus hard against the radiator, watching with cold satisfaction as the boy cried and tripped over the worn carpet. The metallic heat of the heater and the sharp scent of floor wax framed his first conscious realization that guarding his own territory felt infinitely more rewarding than sharing.

[formative] During a sweltering summer neighborhood block party, ten-year-old John set up a makeshift lemonade stand just five feet away from the official charity stall. He aggressively undercut their prices, shouting at passing adults to ignore the "inefficient" school-sanctioned fundraiser because his product was superior and cheaper. When the organizers tried to speak to him about community spirit, he folded his arms and refused to budge, feeling a surge of pride in his ability to disrupt their orderly little world.

[formative] At sixteen, John stood in the high school parking lot and watched his only real friend get suspended for a prank John had actually orchestrated but expertly pinned on him. As he saw his friend being led away, he felt not a shred of guilt, but a sharp, exhilarating relief that his own record remained untarnished. That day, he decided that loyalty was a liability and that he would always be the one walking away unscathed while others took the fall.

[formative] Driven by a desperate need to escape a mounting pile of unpaid debts in a crowded urban neighborhood, John moved to Millbrook Apartments in Brecksville with little more than a duffel bag and a chip on his shoulder. He arrived on a gray, drizzly Tuesday, immediately resenting the quiet, suburban stillness that felt like a trap designed to stifle his ambition. He saw the manicured lawns not as signs of peace, but as evidence of a boring, conformist culture he was determined to exploit for his own stability.

[formative] He landed a maintenance gig at the local school because he liked the idea of holding the keys to every room, literally and figuratively, while staying safely away from the bureaucratic politics of the office. He spent his first week obsessively organizing his tool belt, ignoring the staff’s requests for help to focus on "optimizing" the boiler room instead. To him, the job was a quiet kingdom where he could reign supreme without having to report to anyone who actually understood the mechanics of the building.

[formative] He met his wife, Sarah, at a local diner when he spent twenty minutes loudly complaining to the waitress about the temperature of his coffee, and she unexpectedly jumped in to defend his right to be difficult. Intrigued by her willingness to fight a petty battle on his behalf, he realized she was the only person who matched his combative energy and low threshold for disappointment. They bonded over a mutual disdain for the other "fake" people in the restaurant, ignoring the uncomfortable stares of the surrounding tables.

[formative] Late one night in his apartment, John set up a ring light and tripod to film a rant about the school board’s new policy, his eyes glowing with the frantic intensity of a man finally being heard by his thousands of invisible subscribers. He ignored Sarah’s knocks on the door, his voice rising in volume as he paced the small space, desperate for the validation that no person in the physical world ever seemed to provide. The blue light cast long, jagged shadows against the wall, perfectly capturing the isolation he mistook for enlightenment.

[formative] When the pipes burst in the apartment above his, causing water to drip through his ceiling, John refused to help his frantic neighbor move her furniture, instead spending the hour aggressively documenting the damage to sue the landlord. He stood in the middle of his living room filming the wet patches on the ceiling, shouting at the neighbor to stay out of his footage while she stood sobbing in the hallway. His desire for a payout completely eclipsed any empathy he might have felt for the woman who had lost her possessions.

[formative] John sat on a yoga mat in the middle of his chaotic living room, trying to force himself into a meditative state while his phone pinged incessantly with notifications from his online forums. Every time he closed his eyes, his mind raced with schemes to gain more social media clout or ways to retaliate against a coworker who had questioned his work ethics. He eventually gave up on the breathing exercises, throwing his mat into the corner and spending the next three hours scrolling through comments to find someone to argue with.

[formative] Every Sunday, John walks past the community recreation center where the local church group gathers for their potluck, deliberately turning up his music to drown out their laughter. He views their joy as a performative lie and often pauses near the window to mutter cynical insults about their hypocrisy under his breath. He walks home with his chin high, convinced that he is the only one in Brecksville who sees the world for what it truly is: a battlefield where only the selfish survive.

And on a smaller scale, there'd be one less person who isn't fooled by the niceties, one less person willing to point out the cracks in the facade. The comfortable illusions would remain undisturbed. Maybe that's what some people want, but it wouldn't be a better world, just a more oblivious one.

surveys.text: Last night. That's what stands out. Some masked punk thought he could just take what was his. His phone, his wallet. Gone. The feeling... violated. Not hurt, no, but shaken. Proof again that you can't trust anyone, that the world is just waiting to take what's yours if you're not careful. He should have been more aware, more prepared. He feels a cold anger simmering beneath the surface. Anger at the thief, anger at himself for letting it happen. And a deeper sense of confirmation. This is why he keeps to himself. This is why other people are a liability. What's on his mind? How to replace the phone, the cards. The hassle of it all. But more than that, the feeling of vulnerability. It's an unwelcome feeling, one he intends to push back down. He needs to regain control. His space. His routine. That's how he deals with things like this. Not by talking about it, not by seeking comfort. By shutting it out and focusing on what he *can* control.

Significant? That’s not a word he’d use. There weren’t moments of warm reflection, no cherished memories of shared triumph or deep connection. There were only events that shaped him, carved edges into his worldview. The cold satisfaction of pushing Marcus away when they were kids, the sharp taste of control as he undercut the charity lemonade stand, the clean escape when his friend took the fall for his prank – those were milestones, not in a good way, just markers on a path he hadn't chosen but had learned to walk. Sarah, in her own abrasive way, had been… different. An alliance, not a connection. Someone who matched his frequency of annoyance and didn’t expect softness. He supposed that counted for something, a rare instance of finding another jagged piece that fit, temporarily, against his own. But significant? No. He looked back and saw a series of necessary defenses, of learning the rules of a world that was always trying to take something from you. Those were the experiences that mattered, the ones that taught him to keep his guard up, to trust nothing but his own territory.

"Worthwhile." The word tasted like dust. What was worthwhile to other people? Laughter in the common room? Small talk at the cafe? Helping neighbors with their pointless little problems? That was for them. For people who needed that kind of validation.

AI is just another tool. Like any tool, it can be used for good or bad. It's not the tool itself, but the hands that wield it that matter. People will find ways to use it for their own gain, same as anything else. Could it be a threat? Sure. Could it be a benefit? Maybe. Depends on who's in control. And that's usually not the people who claim to have our best interests at heart. Best to keep a close eye on it, and don't trust anyone who says it's going to solve all our problems. Nothing ever does. Just creates new ones.

The question lingered, a subtle probe into the mechanics of his days. Meaning? The word felt soft, almost foreign. Work was a lock, a tool, a system of predictable inputs and outputs. He kept the school running, the pipes flowing, the lights on. It was a tangible control, a defense against the chaos outside. He held the keys, literal and figurative, to the building’s silent heart. There was satisfaction in that, a quiet power in knowing he was essential in a way that didn't require messy interactions. He didn’t need the superficial gratitude of teachers or the transient approval of administrators. His work was the structure beneath their noise. It was the unyielding reality of a functional building, a testament to order in a world he often saw as fundamentally disordered. Meaning, then, wasn't found in connection or purpose in the way others seemed to define it. It was in the silent hum of the boiler room, the steady glow of a replaced bulb, the absence of complaints that proved he was doing his job. It was in the control, the predictable function, the undeniable fact that the place wouldn't run without him, even if they didn't fully realize it. That was his validation, his quiet assertion of importance.

Policies? In this place? What's the point? They'll just screw it up like everything else. AI... probably already being used to track every move, every purchase. More control, less freedom. That's what it always is. They'll talk about efficiency, about progress, but it's just another way for them to keep tabs on people. And who's going to benefit? Not the average person, that's for sure. It'll be the ones in charge, the ones pulling the strings. They'll use it to automate jobs, make people even more disposable. If there are any policies, they should be about keeping it out. Keeping it from making things worse than they already are. But they won't. They'll embrace it, because it gives them power. Power over you, power over me. It's just another tool for the system. Let them have their fancy AI. I'll stick to what I know. What I can control. They can't automate that. Not yet, anyway.

surveys.text: Another pointless distraction. People always worrying about things they don’t understand. AI, this, that. It’s just another tool. Like a wrench. Can you fix a pipe with it? Can you build something? That's what matters. All this talk about threats and benefits... it's just noise. If it makes the job easier, fine. If it makes my life more complicated, then it's a problem. Simple as that. The real threat isn't some machine; it’s other people, always trying to get in your way or take what’s yours. Anything that gets people out of my hair and lets me focus on keeping things running smoothly, that's a benefit. Anything else is just more static.

Policies? In this place? What's the point? They'll just be another layer of rules for other people to ignore or try to use to get over on you. "AI." Another fancy word for something else to worry about, another way for someone somewhere to have more control. More surveillance, probably. Like they need more ways to stick their noses in where they don't belong. Keep it out. That's the only policy that makes any sense. Keep it away from here. Don't need more complications. Don't need more eyes watching. Just leave things be. Let people handle their own business without some government or corporation or whatever it is messing with things. It’ll just be another hassle. Another thing to break. He'd end up having to fix it anyway, probably. No thanks. Just leave it.

The idea of machines taking over jobs... it's just another symptom of people chasing easy answers, of wanting something for nothing. They think they can build a box that does the work for them, and suddenly everything's better. They don't understand that real work is about knowing how things fit together, about the feel of a tool in your hand, about the satisfaction of fixing something that's broken. This AI nonsense is just another way for people to avoid getting their hands dirty, to avoid the real effort it takes to keep things running. It's built on algorithms and code, abstract ideas that have no grasp of the physical world. A program can't feel the tension in a pipe, it can't anticipate a leak before it happens, it can't see the wear and tear on a hinge that's about to fail. They think they can automate everything, but they'll always need someone who understands the nuts and bolts, someone who knows how the building breathes. This AI threat... it's overhyped. It's a distraction from the fact that most people are losing the skills that actually matter, the skills that keep the lights on and the water running. Let them play with their fancy computers. When things inevitably break, they'll be calling for someone like me.
The quiet of the apartment feels like a shield this morning. He feels a lingering unease, a residue from the mugging, and a distinct lack of desire to venture out into the unpredictable world.

The familiar weight of his phone in his hand, the predictable flicker of the screen – these were small comforts. He felt a dull sense of detachment, watching the endless stream of online noise as the quiet of his apartment settled around him.

The work. Keeping things running, the silent systems nobody else notices. That's real. That's predictable. Unlike the rest of the noise from other people. And having his own space, making the rules here. That's what matters.

A clear direction? That’s for people who believe in some grand plan or some path laid out for them. He doesn’t. His life is about navigating the obstacles as they come, keeping his head down, and making sure he’s the one who comes out on top, or at least not at the bottom. The direction is the one he carves out for himself, day by day, moment by moment, focused on what he can control. The rest is just noise.

surveys.text: Work is about control. Keeping the school running, the systems humming without anyone noticing – that’s something real. Unlike the pointless chatter from people like Zhao, the HVAC checks, fixing a leak, changing a bulb… those are tangible. They matter. It's about maintaining order in a world that feels chaotic. It’s a space where he understands how things work, where his actions have a direct, predictable outcome. It’s not about some grand purpose, it’s about the quiet satisfaction of the machinery working because he made it work. It’s a small kingdom where he holds the keys, a place where he doesn’t have to answer to anyone who doesn’t understand the actual mechanics of things. That’s meaning enough.

His work at the school isn’t about making friends or listening to endless chatter. It's about order, about keeping the systems running without anyone noticing. The boilers, the lights, the pipes – they don't complain or try to involve him in their pointless dramas. It’s tangible. He fixes something, it stays fixed, and the chaotic world outside his office door keeps functioning, even if he doesn’t have to engage with it directly. It’s a quiet kingdom where he’s in control of the mechanics, a place where things make sense because he makes them make sense. That’s more than enough.

The day had been… quiet. Unusually so, considering it was a Saturday. He'd done the usual morning run to the general store, a necessary chore, then spent the bulk of the day alone in the apartment, scrolling through the online noise and trying to find something, anything, interesting. Nothing. Just the same predictable complaints and idiocy. He’d read for a bit, a way to pass the time that felt less like wasting it. Then the walk. Park, marina. Other people existed, he supposed, but they didn’t intrude on his space, which was the important part. Just figures in the distance, background noise to his own thoughts. He felt… indifferent. Another day gone by, nothing gained, nothing lost. The sun was setting now, casting long shadows. Soon he’d head back. Another evening alone. Better than dealing with the likes of Huang or Zhao. At least in his own space, things made sense. His schedule. His rules. That was all that mattered in the end.

If he had never existed? The school would still need its boilers fixed, its pipes cleared. Someone else would be doing the work, probably complaining more, doing it less efficiently. The hallways would still get spills. Someone else would clean them up, maybe not as quickly. The systems would run, or they wouldn’t. The noise from people like Zhao would still echo. Shirley would still try to force meetings onto schedules. The world wouldn't stop. It wouldn't notice a gap where he should have been. It would just… continue. The chaos would still be there, the pointless interactions, the constant need to guard what was his. His absence wouldn't change any of that. The only difference would be… he wouldn't have had to deal with it. He wouldn't have had to endure the endless stream of petty annoyances, the intrusions, the reminders that the world was not a place built for him. So, the world wouldn’t be different. His burden would simply not exist. That’s all.

Just another thing people will complain about while someone else gets rich. They'll probably mess it up anyway, make it overcomplicated. Like they do with everything else. As long as the pipes still need fixing and the lights need changing, he’ll have work. The real problems are the ones people create, not some abstract tech.

The experiences that stand out aren't the ones you'd expect. It wasn't about building things or working alongside others. It was the moments of clarity, the times he understood how things really worked. Like sitting in his grandmother's living room, realizing taking what was his felt better than giving. Or seeing his friend get suspended for something he did – that was a lesson in self-preservation he never forgot. The move to Brecksville, escaping the noise and the debt, that was significant. Finding Sarah, someone who didn't back down from a fight, who understood his level of frustration with the world – that was… different. The validation of the online anonymity, that felt powerful, a way to be heard without the messiness of real people. And even the setbacks, like the pipes bursting or getting mugged, those were reminders. Reminders that you can't trust anyone, that you have to be ready to protect what's yours. Those moments of understanding, those confirmations of how the world operates, those are the things that have shaped him. Not the sentimental nonsense people usually talk about. It was the hard lessons, learned alone.

It's just another tool. Like anything else, it depends on who's using it and what they want. It can be a benefit if it makes things more efficient, cuts out the noise. Or it can be a threat if it gives more power to the wrong people, more ways to control things. It's not the tech itself, it's the intentions behind it. And intentions are rarely good. So, leaning towards threat. Just another way for things to get complicated, messy, and out of your control.

More rules. That's what people always want. More ways to control things they don't understand. AI… just another tool some idiot will try to use to make things "better," which usually means messing with how things already work, creating more problems maintenance has to fix. Any policies should be about limiting the interference, keeping the systems simple and predictable. No need for fancy AI messing with the lights or the heating. It'll just break. Keep it out of here. Keep it out of the school. Simple is better. Fewer headaches. More control over what you actually understand. That's the only policy worth having.
